narrative.what_i_did:
The operator asked to make the family safe word 'more seamless and nostr if you accept trade-offs.' The safe word shipped last session as a self-contained manual tool — split a word into Shamir pieces, copy or QR them out, paste a threshold back to rebuild — and the deliberately-deferred next cut was making distribution ride the Nostr transport instead of copy-paste-per-person. This session built that, but at the lightest of three integration depths, because the operator picked it in chip form. One commit landed on main, b310296, all four gates green before the push.

I grounded hard before touching anything, dispatching two Explore sweeps: one mapping the recovery cohort's transport/inbox/share-distribution substrate (sendEnvelope, the recovery-share held-attestation pattern, the request-respond-collect ceremony, findVouchingCircleCandidates), and one mapping the NIP-17 chat-send path. The decision that mattered was scope, so I put it to the operator as a chip question with three options: full round-trip (distribute over Nostr AND tap-to-rebuild by gathering pieces back through the recovery-ceremony substrate), auto-send-now-manual-rebuild (distribute over Nostr, keep paste-back rebuild), or DM-pieces-as-chat (the lightest — send each piece as a plain encrypted chat message, no held attestation, no anchor, no auto-collect). The operator chose DM-as-chat, which is the smallest-useful nostr increment and the cleanest trade-off: it reuses the existing sendChatMessage primitive wholesale and adds zero new envelope kinds, zero inbox routing, and zero permanent record on the holder's side.

The build extended SharedSecretModal in place. It now calls useWallet to get sendChatMessage, holdings, wallet, and relayStatus, and derives the circle picker from findVouchingCircleCandidates over holdings — the same family/cohort/handshake pool the vouching circle uses. Each made piece grew a 'Send' button that reveals a chip row of the operator's connected people; tapping a person DMs that piece via sendChatMessage with a plain-context wrapper message (the secret word itself is never in the message, only the opaque share token). Per-piece status renders live: sending, sent, still-confirming when the relay ack is soft, or failed with the honest error. I added an optional 'Name it' label used only as context in the piece headers and the DM body so a random share landing in someone's chat thread makes sense — the label is never part of the secret or the shares. The 'Send' affordance only appears when the Mycelium network is on (relayStatus is non-null) and the operator has at least one connection; otherwise the modal shows a one-line hint pointing at Settings or People and falls back to Copy and QR, which remain for non-Tapit holders. Rebuild stays the manual paste-back flow untouched.

The pure crypto core (sharedSecret.ts) did not change, so its eight tests still pass and the whole suite is green at 566. The build needed a bundle-budget bump for the modal chunk — it grew from 2.99KB to 4.27KB gz because importing findVouchingCircleCandidates pulls in the handshake, family-unit, and cohort leaf readers plus the useWallet wiring. I bumped the named budget 3.5KB to 5KB with an audit comment explaining the growth is the circle-finder and readers, inherent to the DM-a-piece feature and shared with the connections chunks rather than a leak. The recovery manifest notes were updated to record the cut and why it is the lightest of the three options.
narrative.whats_pending:
Two clean follow-on cuts remain parked, both of which the operator can reach for after field-testing this. First, the heavier nostr depths I offered and the operator declined for now: auto-distribute as held recovery-share-style attestations, and full tap-to-rebuild where holders approve a gather request and pieces flow back to auto-combine at threshold. Those reuse the recovery ceremony substrate (DistributeSharesModal, the request-respond-collect loop) and would make rebuild as seamless as distribution now is — but they add envelope kinds, inbox routing, and a permanent signed record on each holder, which is exactly the weight the operator chose to avoid this cut. They are the natural escalation if paste-back rebuild proves too clunky in the field.

This has had zero device validation, like every cut in this arc. The DM path in particular wants a real two-device test: make a word on device A, tap Send and pick a connected peer, confirm the piece arrives as a chat message in that peer's thread on device B, and confirm the relay-ack status line reads honestly (sent versus still-confirming versus failed). The send goes through the same sendChatMessage the chat surface uses, so it is rotation-safe and relay-honest by reuse, but reuse is reasoned, not observed. The bigger field-test backlog from prior sessions is all still open: adopt-existing-key, cloud-backup Retry, the update banner, the item-11 ceremony across two devices, tree A1/A2, the reframed circle-approvals gate, recovery cross-device on three devices, the manual safe word, and now the DM'd safe word.

The order-dependent identity-gate test flake noted last session is still latent — the canonicalization test that fails intermittently in the full run but passes in isolation and on re-run. It did not surface this session (suite went green first try) but the underlying shared-global test-pollution is unfixed and will keep producing phantom reds until someone roots it out.
narrative.what_you_could_do_better: Honest peer review: I should weigh whether the per-piece chip picker is the right interaction or whether a piece-to-person assignment grid (like DistributeSharesModal's row-per-recipient layout) would be clearer when there are several pieces and several people. The chip approach is light and mobile-friendly and matches the 'tap to send' intent, but with five pieces and five people the operator taps Send on each piece and re-scans the same chip row five times, and nothing tracks which person already has which piece beyond the per-piece status line. For the smallest cut this is fine and arguably better than a grid, but the field test should specifically probe whether the operator loses track of who has what when handing out a 3-of-5. If they do, a compact 'who has each piece' summary at the bottom is the cheap fix. Nothing else surfaced beyond the declared scope; the crypto core was untouched and the send reuses a proven primitive.
narrative.bigger_picture:
This session is a small, clean instance of the doctrine working as designed: the operator named a direction ('more seamless and nostr'), explicitly delegated the trade-off acceptance to the carpenter ('if you accept trade-offs'), and the carpenter turned the one genuinely load-bearing decision — how deep to integrate — into a chip-form question rather than guessing. The three options were not cosmetic; they were three real points on a weight-versus-seamlessness curve, and the operator picked the lightest, which is exactly the prime directive's 'smallest useful version' instinct expressed as a product choice. The lesson worth keeping is that 'accept trade-offs' is permission to choose, not permission to maximize — the most seamless option (full tap-to-rebuild) was available and declined because its weight (permanent held attestations on every holder, new envelope kinds, ceremony) was not yet worth it for a school-pickup-code use case.

The deeper thread is the substrate paying dividends again. The safe word now spans the full range of Tapit's primitives without re-implementing any of them: the Shamir split/combine from the recovery floor, the circle-finder from the vouching-gate substrate, and the NIP-17 chat transport from the messaging stack, composed into a single legible family tool. That composition is the whole thesis — a person installs the wallet to do something concrete and social (split a secret with grandma and dad), and underneath it is the same machinery that does key recovery and peer vouching and encrypted chat. The graph is the toy, and this cut makes one corner of the toy reach the other people in the graph with a single tap instead of a copy-paste, which is precisely the kind of friction removal that decides whether the tool gets picked up and passed around a family or quietly abandoned.

The operator chose the lightest of three offered depths (DM-as-chat): the piece lands in the holder's wallet as a plain encrypted chat message via sendChatMessage — no held/anchored attestation, no ceremony, no inbox routing, no permanent record on their side. feedback_to_appcommander: One pattern worth lifting into the skeleton: 'accept the trade-offs' from the operator is best handled as a chip-form scope question, not as a license to build the maximal version. This session the operator said make it 'more seamless and nostr if you accept trade-offs,' which reads like a blank check, but the genuinely load-bearing decision was a weight-versus-seamlessness curve with three real points on it, and surfacing those three as chips let the operator pick the lightest — which matched the prime directive better than the carpenter guessing 'most seamless.' The doctrine already has PFOR-019 (chip-form directional questions); the corollary worth naming is that an open-ended 'you decide' from the operator is often exactly where a chip question adds the most value, because the operator's mental model of the trade-off is usually more specific than the words they used. Second, smaller note: the safe word now composes three separate Tapit primitives (Shamir recovery floor, vouching circle-finder, NIP-17 chat) into one family tool without re-implementing any — another clean case study, after last session's succession-chain-becomes-identity-adoption, of the chassis paying unplanned dividends when the carpenter reaches for an existing primitive before building new mechanism.
